questions.title: Positive feedback: labor contractions intensify progressively
questions.subject: fnd
questions.question: Which of the following physiological scenarios is the classic, well-known example of a positive feedback mechanism?

options.A: Uterine contractions becoming progressively stronger and more frequent during labor
options.B: The body shivering to generate heat that has been lost
options.C: Insulin being released to stop rapidly rising blood glucose
options.D: Blood vessels dilating to lower a raised body temperature

explanations.A: Correct. As the fetal head stretches the cervix, oxytocin is released and strengthens uterine contractions, which stretch the cervix further and trigger yet more oxytocin release — the Ferguson reflex — so each cycle amplifies the next, driving the process to completion (delivery) rather than back to a stable set point, the defining feature of positive feedback. This self-reinforcing amplification, rather than a return to a stable baseline, is exactly what marks a loop as positive rather than negative feedback.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Shivering in response to heat loss is a negative feedback response: it corrects a deviation (falling temperature) by driving the variable back toward its normal set point, the opposite pattern from positive feedback.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Insulin release in response to rising glucose is a classic negative feedback loop, lowering glucose back toward its set point rather than amplifying the rise.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vasodilation to lower a raised body temperature is also negative feedback, correcting the deviation back toward the normal set point rather than reinforcing it further.

questions.learning_objective: State that progressively strengthening uterine contractions during labor, mediated by the oxytocin-driven Ferguson reflex, are the classic example of positive feedback, and contrast this with negative feedback.
